(CNN)  -- Despite acknowledgment from the White House a day earlier that a peace deal between Israel and the Palestinians is unlikely before a new U.S. president takes office, Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice said Friday she is confident that ongoing efforts would produce success. Israeli Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni, right, and U.S.  Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice speak Thursday. "Carried to its state of conclusion, it will produce a state of Palestine," Rice, referring to negotiations in the wake of last year's U.S. summit on Israel-Palestinian peace in Annapolis, Maryland, said at a joint news conference with Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas in Ramallah, West Bank. Rice is on her eighth trip to the region since the Annapolis summit. On Thursday, White House spokeswoman Dana Perino said the Bush administration does not "think that it's likely that it (a peace agreement) would happen before the end of the year." Rice said Friday that she realizes the lack of a peace agreement in the months following the Annapolis summit had caused some concerns that talks had stalled or might fail, but "it's quite the opposite -- the Annapolis process has laid the foundation for the eventual establishment for the state of Palestine." The purpose of her current trip, Rice said, was "to advance the Annapolis process," and while she did not speculate on a timetable for the future of the process or offer specifics on peace talks, she added, "I've seen them move forward a great deal in the past year." Both Israeli and Palestinian officials have expressed doubts about achieving a peace agreement before President Bush leaves office, but until this week U.S. officials had been more optimistic in their public comments. Speaking in Israel on Thursday, Rice blamed part of the inability to secure a deal on recent political changes in Israel, which she noted is "in the midst of elections." With Abbas on Friday, she emphasized that the commitment expressed by Abbas and Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert when they signed an agreement to work toward a peace deal by the end of 2008 is still strong. "I hope that the tremendous commitment (by both sides) is fully understood," Rice said. While Rice did not discuss any impact a new administration in Washington might have on the process, she said, "The United States really does understand why the Palestinian people want unity." Israel in recent months has seen political upheaval. Olmert resigned in September amid allegations of corruption. Kadima Party leader and Israeli Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni gave up efforts to form a new coalition government late last month and is seeking to hold early general elections, which could be held in February, Livni's spokesman has said. Olmert will continue to lead as Israel's interim prime minister until a successor assumes power either by forming a coalition in the current Knesset or through general elections. However, it is unclear whether he will be able to strike a deal with the Palestinians before Israel forms its new government. Last month, Rice postponed a trip to a Middle East conference because of the global crisis in financial markets.

**Laying the Groundwork: Condoleezza Rice’s Final Push for Israeli-Palestinian Peace**

As the Bush administration entered its final months, deep skepticism mounted among international observers and regional leaders over whether a comprehensive Israeli-Palestinian peace agreement could be reached. The ambitious timeline established a year earlier was rapidly slipping away, shadowed by political instability in the Middle East and an impending leadership transition in Washington. In response to growing doubts, U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice embarked on a sustained flurry of late-term diplomacy, determined to maintain momentum and salvage the peace process she had worked so hard to revive.

The diplomatic push was anchored in the Annapolis Framework, launched during a high-profile summit in Maryland in November 2007. Annapolis marked the first serious, direct peace negotiations between Israelis and Palestinians in nearly a decade, committing both sides to work toward a two-state solution. However, by late 2008, the political reality on the ground had become increasingly bleak. Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert was hampered by domestic political scandals, while the Palestinian leadership was deeply fractured, with Mahmoud Abbas’s Palestinian Authority governing the West Bank while Hamas maintained control over the Gaza Strip.

Despite these formidable obstacles, Rice engaged in relentless shuttle diplomacy, making repeated trips to Jerusalem, Ramallah, and key regional capitals. Her goal was to push Olmert and Abbas to confront the "final status" issues that had derailed previous peace efforts for generations: defining permanent borders, determining the status of Jerusalem, establishing robust security arrangements, and resolving the plight of Palestinian refugees. 

As the U.S. presidential election approached, Rice and other top U.S. officials publicly acknowledged the reality: a signed, sealed peace treaty would not be finalized before President George W. Bush handed over power to his successor. The political capital of the participating leaders had largely expired, and the ideological gaps on core issues remained too wide to bridge in a matter of weeks.

Nevertheless, Rice firmly rejected the assertion that the diplomatic initiative had been a failure. She argued forcefully that the value of the Annapolis process extended beyond the immediate signature on a document. Through months of intensive, highly detailed, and often confidential negotiations, Israeli and Palestinian teams had engaged on core issues with an unprecedented level of specificity and seriousness. 

Rice asserted that these ongoing talks had accomplished what previous initiatives had not: they had successfully demystified the most complex parameters of the conflict and laid the essential foundation for the ultimate creation of an independent, viable Palestinian state living side-by-side in peace with Israel. 

While the immediate goal of a historic peace deal before the end of the Bush presidency was missed, Rice’s final diplomatic offensive ensured that the negotiations did not end in total collapse. Instead, by defining the narrowest gaps yet between the two sides, her efforts provided a concrete blueprint and a detailed starting point for the incoming U.S. administration and future generations of peacemakers.

**Rice remains optimistic on Middle East peace despite missed 2008 deadline**

**RAMALLAH, West Bank (CNN)** — U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice insisted Thursday that Israelis and Palestinians have made "groundbreaking" progress toward a peace agreement, attempting to strike a hopeful tone during a visit to the West Bank even as Washington openly acknowledged a final deal will not be reached before President George W. Bush leaves office.

Speaking alongside Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas in Ramallah, Rice defended the Annapolis process—launched with great fanfare in Maryland nearly a year ago—which had aimed to secure a historic peace treaty and establish a Palestinian state by the end of 2008.

"I am firmly convinced that the path that was laid at Annapolis... is the path that will ultimately lead to a two-state solution," Rice told reporters. "The work that has been done in the last year is extensive, it is deep, and it has established a foundation that will allow the parties to eventually bridge their remaining differences."

However, Rice’s optimistic posture stood in stark contrast to the sobering reality voiced by the White House earlier in the week. Administration officials formally conceded what diplomats on the ground have privately acknowledged for months: the self-imposed December deadline will pass without a signed agreement.

With President-elect Barack Obama set to take the oath of office on January 20, time has virtually run out for the Bush administration to deliver on its primary foreign policy goal for the Middle East.

**A legacy in the balance**

Rice’s visit to Ramallah marks her eighth trip to the region this year alone, part of a flurry of late-term diplomacy aimed at preserving the momentum of the fragile peace talks. 

Despite the lack of a breakthrough, U.S. officials are pushing both sides to document the points of agreement reached during months of secret negotiations between Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert and President Abbas. The goal, American diplomats say, is to create a baseline for the incoming Obama administration so that future negotiations do not have to start from scratch.

"While we may not reach the finish line by the end of the year, the distance between the two sides has narrowed significantly," Rice said, pointing to improved security coordination in the West Bank and ongoing discussions on core issues, including borders, refugees, and the status of Jerusalem.

Standing beside the Secretary of State, President Abbas praised American efforts but offered a more tempered assessment of the situation on the ground. He expressed deep frustration over continuing Israeli settlement expansion in the West Bank and ongoing military checkpoints, which Palestinians say undermine the peace process and choke their local economy.

"We have exerted every possible effort to reach a peace agreement in 2008," Abbas said through an interpreter. "We have made progress on many issues, but gaps remain. Settlements remain the major obstacle in the way of achieving our shared objective."

**Political hurdles on all sides**

The diplomatic push has been hampered by political volatility in both Israel and the Palestinian territories. 

Olmert, weakened by corruption allegations, serves in a caretaker capacity as Israel prepares for early parliamentary elections scheduled for February 2009. The political uncertainty in Jerusalem makes it nearly impossible for the current Israeli government to make major concessions on sensitive issues like Jerusalem or borders.

Meanwhile, the political schism between Abbas’s Fatah movement in the West Bank and the Islamist militant group Hamas—which violently seized control of the Gaza Strip in 2007—continues to complicate prospects for a unified Palestinian state.

In Washington, White House Press Secretary Dana Perino acknowledged the daunting environment earlier this week, telling reporters that while Bush remains committed to the vision of a Palestinian state, a deal before January is "unlikely."

"We do not believe that it is likely an agreement will be signed by the end of the year," Perino said. "The process is ongoing, but the political dynamics in the region have made a final deal extraordinarily difficult."

**Looking ahead to Obama**

The Quartet of Middle East negotiators—the U.S., Russia, the European Union, and the United Nations—is scheduled to meet in Egypt this weekend to formally review the progress made since the Annapolis summit and to urge both sides to keep talking.

For Rice, the visit represents one of her final opportunities as America’s top diplomat to shape her legacy in the region. Critics argue that the Bush administration engaged in high-level Middle East diplomacy too late in its second term, leaving insufficient time to resolve one of the world's most intractable conflicts.

Rice, however, pushed back against suggestions that the Annapolis effort was a failure.

"Peace is not a single moment; it is a process," Rice said before departing for Jerusalem. "What we have done this year is lay down a firm, indestructible foundation. The dream of a Palestinian state is closer today than it was a year ago."

**RICE MEETS ABBAS IN RAMALLAH AS ISRAELI POLITICAL CRISIS THREATENS FALTERING PEACE TALKS**

**By Middle East Bureau**  
**RAMALLAH, West Bank** — U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice arrived in the West Bank today to hold high-stakes talks with Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas, marking her eighth diplomatic shuttle mission to the region since the landmark Annapolis Peace Conference. However, what was intended as a late-term push to secure a historic Israeli-Palestinian peace framework before the Bush administration leaves office has been severely undermined by deep political instability in Israel, spearheaded by the impending resignation of Prime Minister Ehud Olmert.

Meeting at the presidential compound (*Muqata*) in Ramallah, Rice and Abbas sought to bridge widening gaps between Israeli and Palestinian negotiators on key "core issues"—including the status of Jerusalem, permanent borders, security arrangements, and the right of return for Palestinian refugees. 

Yet, despite Rice’s insistence that both sides remain committed to the process, the atmosphere surrounding the meeting was decidedly muted, overshadowed by the reality that the Israeli government is in a state of political paralysis.

---

### **A Peace Process in Limbo**

The primary shadow hanging over Rice's diplomacy is the downfall of Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert. Plagued by mounting police corruption investigations involving illegal campaign contributions and double-billing schemes, Olmert announced he will step down following his Kadima party's primary elections. 

Olmert’s decision to resign has effectively turned him into a "lame-duck" leader, incapable of delivering the monumental political concessions required for a two-state solution. While Olmert and Abbas had reportedly made incremental progress in private, off-the-record meetings, Israeli opposition figures—led by Likud leader Benjamin Netanyahu—have insisted that a politically compromised prime minister has no legal or moral mandate to negotiate the future of Jerusalem or major West Bank settlement blocks.

"It is very difficult to negotiate a historic peace deal when one of the primary architects is preparing to exit the political stage," said a senior Palestinian negotiator speaking on condition of anonymity. "We are being asked to make final-status concessions to a government that may not exist in a few weeks."

Furthermore, Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni, who leads the Israeli negotiating team, is currently locked in a fierce battle to succeed Olmert as head of Kadima and form a new coalition government. Should she fail, Israel will likely head to early general elections—a process that would freeze all formal peace talks well into next year, far past President George W. Bush’s January 2009 departure from the White House.

---

### **Frustration in Ramallah**

At a joint press conference following their closed-door meeting, President Abbas expressed gratitude for Rice's persistent diplomacy but did not hide his frustration over the lack of tangible progress on the ground. 

Abbas pointed to continued Israeli settlement expansion in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, as well as the network of military checkpoints, as major obstacles that undermine the Palestinian public’s faith in the peace process.

"We have discussed all core issues thoroughly, but time is running out," Abbas told reporters. "Peace cannot be achieved through declarations alone. It requires an Israeli partner capable of fulfilling its obligations under the Road Map, particularly freezing all settlement activity and easing the restrictions on Palestinian movement."

Rice, while acknowledging the severe political challenges in Jerusalem, maintained an optimistic public stance, reiterating the U.S. commitment to establishing an independent Palestinian state existing side-by-side with Israel in peace and security.

"No one ever said this was going to be easy," Rice said. "The political situation in Israel is complex, but the imperative for peace remains unchanged. Both Prime Minister Olmert and President Abbas have demonstrated remarkable leadership, and we will continue to work tirelessly until the end of this administration to achieve our shared goal."

---

### **The Vanishing Window for the Bush Administration**

When President Bush hosted the Annapolis Conference, the declared goal was to reach a comprehensive peace treaty by the end of 2008. Today's meeting highlighted just how unlikely that target has become. 

Beyond Israel's political crisis, the Palestinian leadership remains deeply divided. Abbas’s authority remains largely confined to the West Bank, while the Islamist militant group Hamas continues to maintain total control over the Gaza Strip following its violent takeover. Israeli officials have repeatedly questioned Abbas’s ability to implement any peace agreement in Gaza, further complicating Rice’s diplomatic task.

Middle East analysts note that Rice's eighth visit underscores the paradox of late-stage American diplomacy in the region: a high degree of urgency from Washington, met by severe political domestic constraints on the ground.

"Secretary Rice is trying to build a bridge across a chasm, but the ground on the Israeli side is collapsing due to the coalition crisis, and the ground on the Palestinian side is fractured between Ramallah and Gaza," said Dr. Yossi Alpher, an Israeli political analyst. "Even if Rice, Olmert, and Abbas were to agree on a document today, it would carry little weight with the next Israeli government or the Palestinian street."

As Secretary Rice prepares to travel to Jerusalem to meet with Olmert and Livni before concluding her trip, expectations remain low. While U.S. officials insist that "a foundation is being laid" for future negotiations, the window for a breakthrough under the Bush presidency appears virtually closed, caught in the crossfire of Israel's internal political unraveling.

Speaking to reporters at the State Department, Rice emphasized that despite deep political divisions and persistent violence in the region, a two-state solution remains the only viable path to long-term security for Israel and sovereignty for the Palestinian people.

"The establishment of a peaceful, democratic Palestinian state is not only in the interest of the Palestinians, it is vital to the long-term security of Israel," Rice said. "The time has come to translate our shared vision into reality. It will require leadership, courage, and hard choices on both sides, but the status quo is simply unsustainable."

The White House echoed Rice’s sense of urgency, maintaining that President George W. Bush remains firmly committed to facilitating a diplomatic breakthrough.

White House Press Secretary Dana Perino told reporters during a daily briefing that while the administration acknowledges the monumental hurdles ahead, diplomatic momentum must be sustained.

"Secretary Rice has been working tirelessly on this issue, and the President has full confidence in her efforts," Perino said. "We understand that this is an incredibly complex and emotionally charged process, but both sides know what is at stake. The President believes that peace is achievable if the parties remain focused and stay at the negotiating table."

Rice’s push comes amid intense, behind-the-scenes negotiations between Israeli Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni and Palestinian negotiators. Livni, a leading pragmatic voice within the Israeli cabinet, has emerged as a key figure in the talks, working closely with Washington to navigate sensitive core issues, including final borders, security arrangements, and the status of Jerusalem.

Addressing the progress of those discussions, Rice praised Livni’s strategic approach to the negotiations.

"Foreign Minister Livni has demonstrated remarkable leadership and a clear vision for Israel's future—a future that relies on a stable, peaceful Palestinian state as its neighbor," Rice noted. "She understands that Israel’s security and a two-state solution go hand in hand."

However, significant obstacles continue to threaten the peace process. Israeli officials, including Livni, have consistently stressed that any diplomatic commitment must be tied to rigid security guarantees, particularly regarding rocket fire from the Gaza Strip, which remains under the control of the militant group Hamas. 

At the same time, Palestinian officials argue that ongoing Israeli settlement activity in the West Bank undermines trust and threatens the territorial viability of a future state.

Despite skepticism from critics who question whether a deal can be reached, U.S. officials insisted they will press forward with aggressive diplomatic engagement.

counterfactuals.output:
**JERUSALEM / WASHINGTON** — As the calendar turns toward the final weeks of 2008, U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice is engaged in a high-wire diplomatic race against time. With President George W. Bush’s administration in its final two months, Rice is making a relentless, last-ditch effort to codify progress toward an independent Palestinian state. 

Yet, as Rice shuttles between Jerusalem and Ramallah, her vision of a historic breakthrough is colliding with an unforgiving political reality: an Israeli government in transition, a deeply divided Palestinian leadership, and the impending end of the political era in Washington that launched the renewed effort just one year ago.

### The Promises and Pitfalls of Annapolis

The current diplomatic flurry is the culmination of the process launched at the Annapolis Conference in November 2007, where President Bush convened Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert and Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas. The ambitious goal set at Annapolis was nothing short of a fully negotiated peace treaty establishing a two-state solution by the end of 2008.

Over the past year, Rice has thrown herself into Middle East diplomacy with unprecedented intensity, making nearly two dozen trips to the region. Behind closed doors, Olmert and Abbas have engaged in the most detailed core-issue negotiations since the failed Taba summit in 2001, discussing border adjustments, land swaps, the status of Jerusalem, and the right of return for Palestinian refugees.

Reportedly, Olmert has offered Abbas unprecedented concessions, including a Palestinian state on roughly 93 to 94 percent of the West Bank (supplemented by land swaps), a shared administration for Jerusalem’s holy sites, and a solution for refugees that excludes a broad right of return into Israel proper.

"We are closer than ever before to a real agreement," Rice declared during a recent stop in the region. "The parameters of a two-state solution are clear, and neither side can afford to abandon the progress made."

### Israel’s Political Paralysis

However, Rice’s diplomatic architecture is built on political quicksand in Jerusalem. 

Prime Minister Olmert is a politically crippled leader. Reeling from multiple financial corruption investigations, Olmert announced his intention to resign earlier this year and is now serving merely as a caretaker prime minister. While Olmert remains eager to seal a peace agreement as his political legacy, he lacks the parliamentary majority and moral authority to sign a binding treaty.

The political momentum in Israel has shifted dramatically toward the right. Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni, who succeeded Olmert as head of the centrist Kadima party, failed last month to form a new coalition government. Consequently, Israel is headed for snap parliamentary elections scheduled for February 10, 2009.

Opinion polls consistently show Benjamin Netanyahu, the hawkish leader of the opposition Likud party, holding a commanding lead. Netanyahu has openly criticized the Annapolis framework, dismissing large-scale territorial concessions as a threat to national security and advocating instead for an "economic peace" that focuses on Palestinian institution-building rather than final-status concessions.

Knowing that Netanyahu may soon occupy the Prime Minister's office, Palestinian negotiators are reluctant to make painful concessions to an outgoing Israeli government that cannot guarantee its promises will be honored by the next.

### A Fragmented Palestinian Landscape

The political reality on the Palestinian side is equally grim. The political and geographic schism of June 2007—when the Islamist militant group Hamas violently seized control of the Gaza Strip—continues to severely limit President Abbas’s mandate.

While Abbas governs the West Bank through the Fatah-led Palestinian Authority, Hamas remains in firm control of Gaza. Hamas rejects the two-state parameters being discussed in Jerusalem and views Abbas’s negotiations with Israel as illegitimate. Furthermore, a fragile, Egyptian-brokered six-month ceasefire between Israel and Hamas in Gaza is rapidly fraying, with rocket fire and military incursions threatening a major escalation.

Israeli leaders, including Livni, have repeatedly questioned how Abbas can implement a peace treaty when he exerts no control over half of the potential Palestinian state, creating a fatal bottleneck for any final agreement.

### The Washington Transition: Codifying the "Shelf Agreement"

In Washington, the tectonic plates have already shifted. The election of Barack Obama on November 4 has officially turned the Bush administration into a lame-duck government. While President-elect Obama has signaled a commitment to active Middle East diplomacy, his incoming team will inherit an entirely different global agenda dominated by an unprecedented global financial crisis.

Realizing that a full-fledged peace treaty is now impossible before January 20, 2009, Secretary Rice has recalibrated her goals. Rather than securing a signed treaty, the State Department is now striving for a "shelf agreement"—a documented, joint statement outlining the areas of agreement and convergence achieved over the past year. The idea is to lock in the progress made during the Annapolis process so the incoming Obama administration and the next Israeli government do not have to start from scratch.

Even this reduced ambition faces resistance. Neither Olmert nor Abbas is eager to put their precise positions on paper regarding Jerusalem and borders if a final deal is not guaranteed, fearing it will expose them to severe domestic political blowback without delivering peace.

### An Uncertain Future

As late 2008 slips away, the window for a historic breakthrough during the Bush presidency is effectively closed. 

Secretary Rice’s grueling shuttle diplomacy has proven that the technical parameters of a two-state solution are well understood by leadership on both sides. Yet, her mission highlights a recurring tragedy of Middle East peace negotiations: diplomatic readiness rarely aligns with domestic political alignment.

With Israeli elections looming, Gaza teetering on the brink of conflict, and a political handover underway in Washington, the Annapolis process is ending not with a historic signing ceremony, but with a quiet, anxious waiting game. Whether the progress forged by Rice and her team becomes the blueprint for the next administration—or merely another chapter in a history of missed opportunities—now depends on the political winds of 2009.

### Rice Pushes for Peace in Ramallah Amid Israeli Political Chaos

**By Associated Press / Wire Dispatches**

**RAMALLAH, West Bank** — U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice met with Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas on Tuesday in a bid to keep fragile Middle East peace talks from collapsing, even as deep political turmoil in Israel threatens to derail the Bush administration's final diplomatic push in the region.

Rice’s visit to the West Bank administrative center comes at a critical juncture. Both sides are struggling to meet the ambitious target set at the November 2007 Annapolis summit in Maryland, where President George W. Bush brought Israeli and Palestinian leaders together with a pledge to forge a final peace treaty establishing a Palestinian state before he leaves office in January 2009.

However, the momentum generated at Annapolis has largely stalled, overshadowed by ongoing violence, expanded Israeli settlement construction, and now, a leadership crisis in Jerusalem.

Prime Minister Ehud Olmert, plagued by a series of worsening corruption investigations, announced last month that he will step down following his party's leadership primary in September. The impending departure of Olmert—Rice’s primary Israeli negotiating partner—has effectively turned the Israeli government into a lame duck, casting serious doubt on whether a binding agreement can be reached this year.

Speaking at a joint news conference alongside Abbas in Ramallah, Rice insisted that the diplomatic momentum must continue regardless of the political headwinds in Jerusalem and Washington.

"We have always known that this was going to be a process with ups and downs, but the commitment of the parties to negotiate remains," Rice told reporters. "We continue to work toward the goal that was established at Annapolis, which is to try to reach an agreement by the end of the year."

Abbas expressed deep concern that Israel’s domestic turmoil could freeze negotiations at a crucial moment. Palestinian officials have voiced frustration over the lack of visible progress on core issues, including the borders of a future state, the status of Jerusalem, and the right of return for Palestinian refugees. 

"Time is running short, and the political situation in Israel adds to the complexity," Abbas said through an interpreter. He also reiterated that continued Israeli settlement expansion in the West Bank and East Jerusalem remains a major "obstacle" to the Annapolis vision.

Rice acknowledged Palestinian concerns regarding settlements, stating that U.S. policy regarding expansion had not changed and calling Israeli settlement activity "unhelpful to building the trust necessary" for a breakthrough.

In Washington, the White House sought to play down suggestions that Olmert’s political demise has rendered the Annapolis goals impossible. 

White House Press Secretary Dana Perino told reporters during a briefing that the administration remains realistic about the timeline, but firm in its commitment to the peace framework. 

"We understand that there is a domestic political process playing out in Israel right now," Perino said. "Secretary Rice is over there to help keep the process moving forward. The Israelis and Palestinians signed up for the Annapolis process, and they have committed to negotiating in good faith. That commitment hasn't changed, even if the political calendar is complicated."

Perino added that President Bush remains in regular contact with regional leaders and that the administration believes the fundamental parameters laid out at Annapolis remain the best blueprint for a two-state solution.

Despite the public displays of resolve from Washington and Ramallah, independent analysts and regional diplomats are increasingly skeptical. Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni and Transport Minister Shaul Mofaz are currently vying to replace Olmert as head of the ruling Kadima party. If Livni wins, she will face a grueling period of coalition-building to form a new government, a process that could take weeks or trigger snap general elections—effectively pushing peace negotiations into 2009 and onto the desk of the next U.S. president.

Rice is scheduled to meet with Olmert and Livni in Jerusalem later Tuesday before concluding her 18th trip to the region as Secretary of State.
